question: What is the difference between `var`, `let`, and `const` in JavaScript?
expectedPoints: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted (initialised as `undefined`); `let` and `const` are block-scoped.
`let` can be reassigned; `const` cannot be reassigned after initialisation.
`var` allows redeclaration in the same scope; `let` and `const` do not.
Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): accessing `let`/`const` before declaration throws a ReferenceError.
Prefer `const` by default; use `let` only when the value will change; avoid `var` in modern code.
followUps: Can you mutate an object declared with `const`?
What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
childExplanation: Think of three types of containers. `var` is like writing on a whiteboard in the hallway — anyone walking by can see and change it, and it can be erased and rewritten freely. `let` is like a labelled box in a specific room — only code in that room can use it, and you can swap what's inside. `const` is a sealed box — you can still look inside and even rearrange items within it, but you can never swap the box itself for a different one.
detailedExplanation:
var, let, and const differ in scope, hoisting behaviour, and reassignability. In modern JavaScript you should default to const, use let when you need to reassign, and avoid var.

// --- Scope ---
function demo() {
  if (true) {
    var   a = 1; // function-scoped — visible outside the if block
    let   b = 2; // block-scoped — only inside {}
    const c = 3; // block-scoped + cannot be reassigned
  }
  console.log(a); // 1  ✓
  console.log(b); // ReferenceError ✗
}

// --- Hoisting ---
console.log(x); // undefined (var is hoisted)
var x = 5;

console.log(y); // ReferenceError — TDZ (let/const hoisted but not initialised)
let y = 5;

// --- const with objects ---
const obj = { name: 'Alice' };
obj.name = 'Bob'; // ✓ mutation is fine
obj = {};            // ✗ TypeError — rebinding is not allowed
Classic Trap

const does not make a value immutable — it only prevents rebinding the variable. An object or array declared with const can still have its properties or elements changed. To deeply freeze an object use Object.freeze().

Follow-up

"Why does var in a for loop cause bugs with async callbacks?" — All loop iterations share the same var binding. By the time the callback fires, the loop has finished and the variable holds its final value. Switching to let creates a fresh binding per iteration, fixing this.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer each question before expanding the answer.

  1. 1What exactly is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) and why does it exist?
    The TDZ is the period between entering a block scope and the line where let/const is declared. The variable exists (it was hoisted) but is not yet initialised — accessing it throws a ReferenceError. The TDZ was introduced to catch bugs where code accidentally uses a variable before it logically exists.
  2. 2Classic closure-in-loop: why does `var i` in a `for` loop with `setTimeout` always log the final value?
    With var, there is only one i shared across all iterations. The setTimeout callback closes over that single variable, not its value at the time of creation. By the time the callbacks fire, the loop has incremented i to its terminal value. Using let gives each iteration its own binding, so each callback captures the correct value.
  3. 3When would you intentionally use `var` in modern code?
    Rarely — almost never. The only edge case is when you genuinely need function-scoped hoisting across multiple blocks, but modern patterns (hoisting the let declaration to the top of the function) achieve the same without var's footguns. In legacy code you may encounter it; in new code, prefer let/const.
  4. 4How do you make an object truly immutable (not just prevent rebinding)?
    Object.freeze(obj) prevents adding, removing, or changing properties on the top level. For deep immutability you must recursively freeze nested objects, or use a library like Immer. In TypeScript, Readonly<T> and as const provide compile-time immutability checks without runtime overhead.

question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined` in JavaScript?
expectedPoints: `undefined` means a variable has been declared but not yet assigned a value.
`null` is an intentional assignment representing 'no value' or 'empty'.
`typeof undefined` is `'undefined'`; `typeof null` is `'object'` (a known JS quirk).
`null == undefined` is `true` (loose equality), but `null === undefined` is `false`.
Use `null` to explicitly clear a value; `undefined` usually appears automatically.
followUps: When would you explicitly set a variable to `null`?
How do optional chaining (`?.`) and nullish coalescing (`??`) relate to these?
childExplanation: Imagine a parking space. `undefined` is a space that has never been assigned to anyone — it's blank on the booking sheet. `null` is a space that someone has intentionally marked as 'available / empty' after the previous car left. Both are empty, but `undefined` means 'nothing was ever put here', while `null` means 'I deliberately set this to nothing'.
detailedExplanation:
Both null and undefined represent absence of a value, but they come from different sources. undefined is what JavaScript assigns automatically when a variable, parameter, or property has no value. null must be set explicitly by the programmer.

// undefined — appears automatically
let a;                        // undefined
function greet(name) { return name; }
greet();                    // name is undefined
const obj = {};
console.log(obj.missing); // undefined

// null — set intentionally
let user = fetchUser();     // null = "no user found"

// typeof quirk
console.log(typeof undefined); // 'undefined'
console.log(typeof null);      // 'object' ← historic JS bug

// equality
console.log(null == undefined);  // true  (loose)
console.log(null === undefined); // false (strict)
Classic Trap

typeof null === 'object' is a long-standing JavaScript bug that cannot be fixed without breaking the web. Never use typeof to check for null — use a strict equality check: value === null.

Follow-up

The nullish coalescing operator ?? only treats null and undefined as missing — unlike ||, which also short-circuits on 0, '', and false. Use ?? when those falsy values are valid.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why does `null == undefined` return true, but `null === undefined` return false?
    The ECMAScript spec defines null == undefined as true as a special case of loose equality — the two are considered equivalent "nullish" values. Strict equality (===) requires the same type, and null (type: null) differs from undefined (type: undefined).
  2. 2What is the difference between `||` and `??` for default values?
    || uses any falsy value (0, '', false, null, undefined) to trigger the fallback. ?? only triggers on null or undefined. Use ?? when 0 or empty string are valid values you want to keep.
  3. 3How does optional chaining (`?.`) handle null and undefined?
    obj?.prop short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing a TypeError when obj is null or undefined. It is useful for deeply nested property access: user?.address?.city safely returns undefined if any part of the chain is nullish.

quiz.explanation: `typeof null` returns `'object'` — a well-known historical bug in JavaScript that has never been fixed to avoid breaking existing code. Always use strict equality (`=== null`) to check for null.

question: What is a callback function in JavaScript and why is it useful?
expectedPoints: A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later.
Callbacks enable asynchronous patterns — e.g., reacting to a click event or a completed fetch.
Array methods like `forEach`, `map`, and `filter` accept callbacks.
Common pitfall: callback hell — deeply nested callbacks that reduce readability.
Promises and `async/await` were introduced partly to address callback hell.
followUps: What is callback hell and how do Promises solve it?
Can you write a function that accepts and invokes a callback?
childExplanation: Imagine ordering a pizza and giving the restaurant your phone number so they can call you when it's ready. You don't stand at the counter waiting — you go do other things. When the pizza is done, they 'call you back'. In JavaScript, a callback is a function you hand to another function so it can be called when some work finishes.
detailedExplanation:
A callback is simply a function passed as an argument. The receiving function calls it at the right time — immediately, after a delay, or when an async operation completes.

// Synchronous callback — called immediately
[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => console.log(n));

// Asynchronous callback — called later
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log('1 second later');
}, 1000);

// Custom function that accepts a callback
function doWork(data, onDone) {
  const result = data.toUpperCase();
  onDone(result); // invoke the callback
}
doWork('hello', (r) => console.log(r)); // 'HELLO'

// Callback hell — avoid this
getUser(id, (user) => {
  getPosts(user, (posts) => {
    getComments(posts[0], (comments) => {
      // deeply nested — hard to read/debug
    });
  });
});
Pitfall

Callback hell (also called the 'pyramid of doom') occurs when async operations are chained by nesting callbacks. The code becomes difficult to read and error-prone. Use Promises or async/await to flatten the chain.

Follow-up

Array higher-order methods (map, filter, reduce) all accept callbacks. Understanding callbacks is the foundation for understanding these methods and for grasping Promises, which wrap callbacks in a cleaner API.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What is the difference between a synchronous and an asynchronous callback?
    A synchronous callback is invoked immediately within the calling function before it returns — e.g., the callback in Array.forEach runs inline. An asynchronous callback is invoked later, after some operation (timer, network request, I/O) completes — e.g., the callback in setTimeout or fs.readFile. The calling function returns before the callback runs.
  2. 2How do Promises solve callback hell?
    Promises allow chaining with .then() instead of nesting. Each .then() receives the result of the previous step and returns a new Promise, keeping the code flat and readable. A single .catch() at the end handles errors from any step — unlike callbacks where each level needs its own error handling.
  3. 3What is the difference between `map` and `forEach`?
    map returns a new array of the same length with each element transformed by the callback. forEach returns undefined — it is used for side effects only (logging, DOM updates). Use map when you need a transformed array; use forEach when you only need to iterate.

quiz.explanation: `Array.map()` invokes its callback synchronously for each element before returning. `setTimeout`, `fetch().then()`, and `addEventListener` callbacks are all asynchronous — they run after the current call stack is clear.

question: What are arrow functions in JavaScript and how do they differ from regular functions?
expectedPoints: Arrow functions use the `() => {}` syntax and are more concise than `function` declarations.
Arrow functions do NOT have their own `this`; they inherit `this` from the surrounding lexical scope.
Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors (no `new`).
Arrow functions have no `arguments` object.
Best used for short callbacks; avoid as object methods where `this` needs to refer to the object.
followUps: Why can't you use an arrow function as a method that needs `this`?
What does 'lexical `this`' mean?
childExplanation: Think of a regular function as an employee who has their own name badge and desk — they have their own identity (`this`). An arrow function is like a contractor who doesn't have their own desk — they sit at whoever hired them's desk and use that identity. This is handy inside callbacks, but causes confusion when you need the function to have its own identity as an object method.
detailedExplanation:
Arrow functions are a concise syntax introduced in ES6. The key behavioural difference from regular functions is how this is resolved: regular functions set this dynamically based on how they are called; arrow functions capture this lexically from the enclosing scope at the time they are defined.

// Syntax comparison
const add = function(a, b) { return a + b; };
const add = (a, b) => a + b; // implicit return

// `this` — where arrows shine
class Timer {
  constructor() { this.seconds = 0; }
  start() {
    // Arrow inherits `this` from start() — correct
    setInterval(() => { this.seconds++; }, 1000);
    // Regular function would have `this` === undefined (strict) or window
  }
}

// `this` — where arrows hurt
const obj = {
  name: 'Alice',
  greet: () => console.log(this.name), // ✗ `this` is outer scope, not obj
  greetOk() { console.log(this.name); }  // ✓ regular method
};
Common Mistake

Using an arrow function as an object method or class method that references this. Because arrows inherit this from the outer scope (often the module or undefined in strict mode), this.name will not refer to the object. Always use regular method shorthand syntax inside object literals and classes.

Follow-up

Arrow functions have no arguments object. If you need to collect all arguments, use a rest parameter: const fn = (...args) => args. Arrow functions also cannot be generators (function*).

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What does 'lexical this' mean and why does it matter?
    Lexical this means the value of this is determined by where the function is written in the source code (its lexical position), not by how it is called. For arrow functions, this is the same as the enclosing scope's this at definition time and cannot be changed with .call(), .apply(), or .bind().
  2. 2Can you change the `this` of an arrow function using `.bind()`?
    No. .bind(), .call(), and .apply() cannot override the lexical this of an arrow function. Calling arrowFn.bind(obj) returns the same arrow function with this unchanged. This is by design — it makes arrow functions predictable inside callbacks.
  3. 3When should you use a regular function vs an arrow function in React?
    In React functional components, arrow functions work well for event handlers and callbacks inside JSX (e.g., onClick={() => setCount(c + 1)}) because you don't need a dynamic this. Use regular function declarations for top-level component functions or custom hooks — mainly for clarity and hoisting. Avoid creating arrow functions inline inside useCallback if the reference stability matters.

question: What is event bubbling in the DOM and how do you stop it?
expectedPoints: When an event fires on an element, it first runs handlers on that element, then bubbles up through ancestors.
Example: clicking a `<button>` inside a `<div>` triggers the button's handler, then the div's.
`event.stopPropagation()` prevents the event from bubbling further.
Event delegation uses bubbling beneficially — attach one listener on a parent to handle events from many children.
`event.preventDefault()` stops the browser's default action but does NOT stop bubbling.
followUps: What is event delegation and when is it useful?
What is the difference between bubbling and capturing phase?
childExplanation: Imagine dropping a pebble in a pond — the ripple starts at the point of impact and spreads outward in circles. In the DOM, a click event starts at the element you clicked and 'ripples' up through every parent element until it reaches the document. Each parent that has a listener for that event will hear it, just like each circle in the ripple grows wider.
detailedExplanation:
DOM events travel in three phases: capture (down from document to target), target, then bubble (back up to document). By default, most event listeners run during the bubble phase.

<!-- HTML -->
<div id="outer"><button id="btn">Click</button></div>

// Both handlers fire on a button click (bubbling)
document.getElementById('btn').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  console.log('button clicked');
});
document.getElementById('outer').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  console.log('div also fires!'); // runs due to bubbling
});

// Stop bubbling
document.getElementById('btn').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  e.stopPropagation(); // div listener will NOT fire
});

// Event delegation — one listener handles all children
document.getElementById('outer').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  if (e.target.matches('button')) {
    console.log('a button inside outer was clicked');
  }
});
Common Confusion

e.preventDefault() and e.stopPropagation() do different things. preventDefault() stops the browser's built-in response (e.g., following a link, submitting a form) but the event still bubbles. stopPropagation() stops the event from travelling further up the DOM but does not cancel the browser's default action.

Follow-up

Event delegation leverages bubbling to handle events efficiently. Instead of attaching a listener to each of 1,000 list items, attach one listener to the parent <ul> and check e.target to identify which child was clicked. This is especially useful for dynamically added elements.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What is the difference between `e.target` and `e.currentTarget`?
    e.target is the element that originally triggered the event (where the click landed). e.currentTarget is the element whose listener is currently running — which may be an ancestor if the event has bubbled. In event delegation, e.target is the child that was clicked, while e.currentTarget is the parent with the listener.
  2. 2What is the capturing phase and how do you listen during it?
    The capturing phase travels from the document root down to the target, before bubbling begins. Pass { capture: true } as the third argument to addEventListener to listen during capture. Capturing is rarely needed in practice — most UI frameworks and patterns rely on bubbling.
  3. 3When is event delegation NOT a good idea?
    Avoid delegation when: (1) the event does not bubble (e.g., focus, blur, scroll — use focusin/focusout instead); (2) the child elements are deeply nested and e.target matching becomes complex; (3) you need very precise control over which element's handler runs. Also avoid when stopPropagation is called inside a child, preventing the event from reaching the delegated parent listener.

question: What is the difference between props and state in React?
expectedPoints: Props are passed from a parent component and are read-only inside the receiving component.
State is managed inside a component and can change over time using `useState`.
When state changes, React re-renders the component; when props change, the child re-renders.
Props enable parent-to-child data flow; state enables a component to track its own data.
A component should never mutate its own props.
followUps: When would you lift state up to a parent component?
What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components?
childExplanation: Think of a component as a vending machine. Props are like the coins you insert from outside — the machine cannot mint its own coins or change the ones you gave it. State is like the internal counter inside the machine that tracks how many items are left — only the machine itself updates that number, and whenever it changes, the machine reacts (re-renders its display).
detailedExplanation:
Props (short for properties) flow from parent to child and are immutable inside the child. State is local, mutable data owned by a component. Changing state triggers a re-render.

// Props — passed from parent, read-only in child
function Greeting({ name }) {       // name is a prop
  return <h1>Hello, {name}</h1>;
}
// <Greeting name="Alice" />

// State — owned by the component, can change
import { useState } from 'react';
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
      Clicked {count} times
    </button>
  );
}

// Using both: parent holds state, passes as prop
function App() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState('Alice');
  return <Greeting name={user} />; // state flows as prop
}
Common Mistake

Never mutate props directly inside a child component. If you find yourself wanting to change a prop, the real solution is to lift the state up to the parent and pass a setter function as a prop (a callback pattern). Mutating props causes unpredictable behaviour because React won't know the data changed.

Follow-up

"When do you lift state up?" — When two sibling components need to share the same piece of data, move that state to their closest common ancestor and pass it down as props. This keeps a single source of truth.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What happens to the UI when you call a state setter?
    React schedules a re-render. On the next render, the component function runs again with the new state value. React then compares the new output with the previous one (reconciliation) and updates only the changed DOM nodes. State updates are batched in React 18 — multiple setters in one event handler trigger a single re-render.
  2. 2Can you pass a function as a prop? Why would you?
    Yes. Passing a function as a prop is the standard way to allow a child to communicate back to a parent — often called a "callback prop". For example, <Button onClick={handleClick} />. The child calls the function; the parent handles the state update. This keeps state ownership in the parent.
  3. 3What is the difference between initialising state with a value vs a function?
    useState(expensiveComputation()) runs the computation on every render, even though only the first result is used. useState(() => expensiveComputation()) (lazy initialisation) only calls the function on the first render. Use the function form when the initial state is expensive to compute.

question: What is JSX and why does React use it?
expectedPoints: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript.
Browsers cannot read JSX directly — Babel compiles it to `React.createElement()` calls.
JSX makes component templates more readable and co-located with their logic.
Differences from HTML: `className` instead of `class`, `htmlFor` instead of `for`, camelCase event handlers.
Expressions can be embedded inside JSX using `{}`.
followUps: What does Babel compile JSX into?
Can you use React without JSX?
childExplanation: JSX is like a special shorthand note that your computer translates into real instructions. Imagine writing a recipe using simple icons instead of full sentences — it's much faster to read and write. A tool called Babel reads your JSX and converts it into standard JavaScript that the browser understands, just like translating the icons back into full sentences.
detailedExplanation:
JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It looks like HTML but lives inside a .jsx or .tsx file and gets compiled to React.createElement() calls before the browser ever sees it. The compilation is done by Babel (or the TypeScript compiler in TSX files).

// JSX you write
const el = <h1 className="title">Hello</h1>;

// What Babel compiles it to
const el = React.createElement('h1', { className: 'title' }, 'Hello');

// Embedding expressions with {}
const name = 'Alice';
const el = <p>Hello, {name}!</p>; // Hello, Alice!

// JSX vs HTML differences
<div className="box">       // class → className
  <label htmlFor="inp">  // for   → htmlFor
  <input onChange={fn} /> // camelCase events
</div>
Common Mistakes

Using class instead of className (reserved word in JS), or for instead of htmlFor. Also, JSX expressions must return a single root element — wrap siblings in a <Fragment> (or <></>) if you need to return multiple elements without adding an extra DOM node.

Follow-up

You can use React without JSX by calling React.createElement directly, but it quickly becomes verbose and hard to read. JSX was designed specifically to make component trees look like the HTML they produce, improving developer experience.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why must JSX return a single root element?
    Because JSX compiles to React.createElement(), which returns a single object. A function can only return one value. Wrapping in <></> (Fragment) compiles to React.createElement(React.Fragment, ...), which is a single element that adds no DOM node.
  2. 2Can you use `if` statements inside JSX?
    Not directly inside the JSX expression — JSX only allows expressions (things that produce a value), not statements. Use the ternary operator (condition ? a : b) or short-circuit evaluation (condition && <Component />) inside JSX. Full if/else blocks can be used outside JSX to compute a variable, which is then referenced inside JSX.
  3. 3What is the `key` prop and why does React require it for list rendering?
    When rendering a list with .map(), React needs to identify which element is which across re-renders to make efficient DOM updates. The key prop is a unique, stable identifier (ideally a database ID) that React uses internally for reconciliation. Without it, React falls back to index-based comparison, which causes bugs when the list is reordered.

question: Why is the `key` prop important when rendering lists in React?
expectedPoints: React uses `key` to identify which items in a list have changed, been added, or removed.
Without a stable `key`, React may re-render items unnecessarily or produce incorrect UI.
Keys should be unique among siblings and stable — prefer database IDs over array indices.
Using the array index as a key causes bugs when the list is reordered or items are inserted.
Keys are not passed as props to the component — they are only used by React internally.
followUps: What problems arise from using array indices as keys?
Does `key` need to be globally unique or just unique among siblings?
childExplanation: Imagine a classroom where every student has a name tag. When the teacher rearranges the seats, she can quickly find each student by their name — not by which seat number they were sitting in before. Without name tags, she'd have to guess who's who based on position, leading to mistakes. React's `key` prop is the name tag that tells React which item is which, even after the list is shuffled.
detailedExplanation:
During reconciliation React compares the current and previous render outputs. For lists, it needs a stable identifier to match old items to new ones efficiently. Without key, React uses position, which fails when items are reordered or inserted.

// ✗ Bad — index as key (breaks on reorder/insert)
{items.map((item, i) => (
  <li key={i}>{item.name}</li>
))}

// ✓ Good — stable unique ID from data
{items.map((item) => (
  <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>
))}

// key is NOT passed as a prop — child cannot read it
function Card({ id, name }) {
  // props.key is undefined — pass id separately if needed
  return <div>{name}</div>;
}
Index as Key

If you insert an item at the top of a list, every element's index shifts. React sees that index 0 now has different content and re-renders every item — and may lose input state (e.g., a typed value in a text field) because it thinks item 0 is the same element as before. Use stable IDs from your data.

Follow-up

Keys only need to be unique among siblings in the same list — not globally across the entire app. The same key value can be used in a completely different list without conflict.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1When is it actually safe to use the array index as a key?
    It is safe when: (1) the list is static and will never be reordered or filtered; (2) the items have no internal state (no inputs, no animations); (3) there is no stable unique ID available. Even then, it is better to generate a unique ID when creating the data. The official React docs describe this scenario explicitly.
  2. 2How can using a key force a component to fully reset?
    Changing a component's key causes React to unmount the old instance and mount a completely new one, resetting all state. This is a useful pattern: <Form key={userId} /> — changing userId resets the form completely without needing a useEffect.

question: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components in React?
expectedPoints: A controlled component has its form value managed by React state (`value` + `onChange`).
An uncontrolled component stores its own value in the DOM; you read it via a `ref`.
Controlled components give React full control, making validation and conditional logic easy.
Uncontrolled components are simpler for basic cases like file inputs.
The React documentation recommends controlled components for most form use cases.
followUps: When would you prefer an uncontrolled component?
How does `useRef` help with uncontrolled inputs?
childExplanation: A controlled input is like a puppet — React holds the strings. Every keystroke flows through React state: React decides what the input shows. An uncontrolled input is like a free actor — it manages its own value in the DOM and you only check in when you need the final result (for example, when the form is submitted).
detailedExplanation:
In a controlled component, the input's value is driven by React state. Every keystroke fires onChange, which updates state, which re-renders the input with the new value. In an uncontrolled component, the DOM owns the value and you use a ref to read it imperatively.

// Controlled — React drives the value
function ControlledInput() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  return (
    <input
      value={text}                         // driven by state
      onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}

// Uncontrolled — DOM owns the value
function UncontrolledInput() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);
  function handleSubmit() {
    console.log(inputRef.current.value); // read on demand
  }
  return <input ref={inputRef} defaultValue="" />;
}
Common Mistake

Setting value without an onChange handler makes the input read-only and React will warn you. If you only want to set an initial value without controlling it, use defaultValue instead of value.

Follow-up

File inputs (<input type="file">) are always uncontrolled in React because their value is read-only by browser security rules — you cannot programmatically set the selected file. Use a ref to access inputRef.current.files.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why does React warn when `value` is set without `onChange`?
    When value is set, React takes control of the input. Without onChange, the value never updates — the user can type but the input immediately reverts to the last state value, appearing frozen. React warns because this almost always indicates a bug: either add onChange to make it truly controlled, or switch to defaultValue for uncontrolled behaviour.
  2. 2When would you prefer a form library like React Hook Form over manual controlled inputs?
    For complex forms with many fields, controlled inputs re-render the component on every keystroke — manageable for one input, but expensive for 20. React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs internally and only re-renders on submit or validation, dramatically improving performance. Use it for forms with: many fields, complex validation, or frequent real-world user input.

question: What is the `useEffect` hook in React and when do you use it?
expectedPoints: `useEffect` runs side effects after the component renders — e.g., data fetching, subscriptions, timers.
The dependency array controls when it re-runs: empty `[]` runs once on mount, no array runs every render.
The optional cleanup function (returned from `useEffect`) runs before the component unmounts or before the effect re-runs.
Common use cases: fetch on mount, subscribe to an event, update the document title.
Avoid putting everything in `useEffect` — prefer derived state or event handlers where possible.
followUps: What happens if you omit the dependency array entirely?
Why is the cleanup function important for subscriptions?
childExplanation: Imagine `useEffect` as a sticky note you leave for yourself on the front door: 'When I get home, do X.' The component renders (you arrive home), and then React reads your sticky note and performs the effect. If you have a cleanup step, it's another note: 'Before you leave again, undo X first.' The dependency array is the condition on the note: 'only do this if certain things changed since last time.'
detailedExplanation:
useEffect separates rendering (pure, produces JSX) from side effects (anything that interacts with the outside world). It always runs after the browser has painted, so it never blocks the UI.

// Runs once on mount (empty dep array)
useEffect(() => {
  fetchUser(id).then(setUser);
}, []); // [] = run once

// Runs every time `count` changes
useEffect(() => {
  document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
}, [count]); // re-runs when count changes

// With cleanup — unsubscribe before re-run or unmount
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => tick(), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id); // cleanup
}, []);

// No dep array — runs after EVERY render (rarely useful)
useEffect(() => { console.log('rendered'); });
Common Mistake

Forgetting cleanup causes memory leaks and stale callbacks. If you subscribe to an event, start a timer, or open a WebSocket inside useEffect, always return a cleanup function that undoes it. React calls cleanup before the component unmounts and before the next time the effect runs.

Follow-up

In React 18 Strict Mode (development only), effects run twice on mount to help detect missing cleanup. If you see your effect firing twice, that's expected in development — it won't happen in production.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What is a stale closure in `useEffect` and how do you fix it?
    A stale closure happens when an effect captures a state or prop value at the time it was created, but that value has since changed. The effect still holds the old value. Fix it by adding the variable to the dependency array so the effect re-runs with the fresh value, or use a ref to store the latest value without re-running the effect.
  2. 2When should you use `useLayoutEffect` instead of `useEffect`?
    useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints — use it when you need to read or modify the DOM (e.g., measure an element's size) before the user sees any update. useEffect runs after paint, so if you update the DOM there the user may see a flicker. Prefer useEffect for everything else — useLayoutEffect can hurt performance if overused.
  3. 3Should you fetch data in `useEffect`? What are the alternatives?
    Fetching in useEffect works but has pitfalls: no built-in caching, no deduplication, race conditions (response arrives after unmount), and boilerplate. Alternatives: React Query / TanStack Query (handles caching, deduplication, background refetch) or Next.js Server Components (fetch on the server, no client effect needed). For new code, prefer a data-fetching library over raw useEffect.

question: What is the DOM and how does JavaScript interact with it?
expectedPoints: The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree-like representation of an HTML document created by the browser.
Each HTML element becomes a node in the tree; JavaScript can read and modify these nodes.
Common APIs: `document.getElementById`, `querySelector`, `createElement`, `addEventListener`.
Modifying the DOM can trigger reflow and repaint, which are expensive — batch DOM changes when possible.
Frameworks like React abstract direct DOM manipulation through a virtual DOM.
followUps: What is the difference between the DOM and the HTML source?
Why is direct DOM manipulation expensive?
childExplanation: When the browser reads your HTML file, it builds a family tree from it — parents, children, and siblings. This tree is called the DOM. JavaScript can walk this tree, find any member of the family, change their properties, add new members, or remove them. Every time you change a node, the browser has to redraw part of the page — so it's like repainting a room every time you move a piece of furniture.
detailedExplanation:
The browser parses HTML and constructs the DOM tree in memory. JavaScript interacts with the DOM through the document object — a global entry point to the entire tree.

// Reading from the DOM
const el  = document.getElementById('title');
const btn = document.querySelector('button.primary');
const all = document.querySelectorAll('li'); // NodeList

// Modifying the DOM
el.textContent = 'New title';
el.classList.add('highlighted');
el.style.color = 'red';

// Creating and inserting nodes
const li = document.createElement('li');
li.textContent = 'New item';
document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(li);

// Listening for events
btn.addEventListener('click', () => alert('clicked!'));
Performance

Every DOM change can trigger a reflow (recalculating layout) and repaint (redrawing pixels). Reading layout properties like offsetHeight after writing forces a synchronous reflow (layout thrashing). Batch writes together and avoid interleaving reads and writes in a loop. This is one reason React batches state updates.

Follow-up

The DOM is not the same as the HTML source. JavaScript can add, remove, and modify nodes at runtime — so the DOM can differ significantly from the original HTML file. "View Source" shows the original HTML; browser DevTools inspector shows the live DOM.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What is the difference between `innerHTML` and `textContent`?
    innerHTML gets or sets the HTML markup inside an element — it parses the string as HTML, allowing tags. textContent gets or sets the raw text — all HTML tags are treated as plain text. Using innerHTML with user-supplied data is a major XSS risk; prefer textContent for any user-generated content.
  2. 2What is a virtual DOM and how does it improve performance?
    A virtual DOM is an in-memory JavaScript representation of the real DOM. React builds a new virtual tree on each render, diffs it against the previous tree (reconciliation), and only applies the minimal set of real DOM changes needed. This avoids unnecessary reflows and repaints — touching the real DOM only where the output actually changed.

question: What is the CSS box model and what are its four components?
expectedPoints: Every element is a rectangular box composed of: content, padding, border, and margin.
Content: the actual text or child elements inside the element.
Padding: space between the content and the border (shares the element's background color).
Border: a visible or invisible line around the padding.
Margin: space outside the border, separating the element from its neighbours.
`box-sizing: border-box` makes `width`/`height` include padding and border, simplifying layout.
followUps: What is the difference between `box-sizing: content-box` and `border-box`?
What is margin collapsing?
childExplanation: Think of every HTML element as a gift box: the gift itself is the content, the tissue paper wrapping it is the padding, the cardboard box walls are the border, and the gap between this box and the next one on the shelf is the margin. The total space the box takes up depends on all four layers added together — unless you use border-box sizing, which promises a fixed outer box size no matter how thick the walls or padding are.
detailedExplanation:
Every HTML element is rendered as a rectangular box with four concentric layers. Understanding the box model is essential for predictable layout.

/* Default: box-sizing: content-box */
/* width/height = content only */
.box {
  width: 200px;    /* content width */
  padding: 20px;   /* adds 40px total */
  border: 2px solid; /* adds 4px total */
  /* actual rendered width = 200 + 40 + 4 = 244px */
}

/* border-box: width includes padding + border */
.box {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: 200px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 2px solid;
  /* actual rendered width = 200px exactly */
}

/* Global reset — used by almost every project */
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
Common Confusion

The default box-sizing: content-box means adding padding or border increases the total rendered size beyond what you set for width. This causes elements to overflow containers unexpectedly. Most modern CSS resets (and frameworks like Tailwind) apply box-sizing: border-box globally to avoid this.

Follow-up

Margin collapsing: vertical margins between adjacent block elements collapse into a single margin equal to the larger of the two. For example, a paragraph with margin-bottom: 20px above another with margin-top: 10px will produce a 20px gap, not 30px. This does not apply to horizontal margins or flex/grid children.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does `outline` differ from `border` in the box model?
    outline is drawn outside the border and does not affect layout — it takes up no space and cannot cause other elements to shift. border is part of the box model and does affect the element's rendered size (in content-box mode). Outlines are often used for focus indicators because they don't disturb layout.
  2. 2What causes margin collapsing, and when does it NOT happen?
    Margin collapsing occurs between adjacent sibling block elements' vertical margins and between a parent and its first/last child when there is no border, padding, or formatting context between them. It does NOT happen with: flex or grid children, elements with overflow other than visible, floated or absolutely positioned elements, or inline elements.

question: How does CSS Flexbox work and what problems does it solve?
expectedPoints: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system — it lays items in a row or column.
Applied with `display: flex` on the container; children become flex items.
Key container properties: `flex-direction`, `justify-content` (main axis), `align-items` (cross axis), `flex-wrap`.
Key item properties: `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, `flex-basis`, `align-self`.
Solves classic problems: vertically centering an element, distributing space evenly, equal-height columns.
followUps: When would you use CSS Grid instead of Flexbox?
What does `justify-content: space-between` do?
childExplanation: Flexbox is like an adjustable shelf organizer. You decide whether to arrange items side by side (row) or stacked (column), how to spread them out (space-between, space-around), and how to line them up vertically within the shelf (align-items). Each item can also control its own size with flex-grow — greedy items can grow to fill leftover space while others stay their natural size.
detailedExplanation:
Flexbox solves the one-dimensional layout problem: distributing items along a single axis (row or column) with alignment control on both axes.

/* Centering — the classic use case */
.container {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center; /* main axis  (horizontal in row) */
  align-items: center;    /* cross axis (vertical in row)   */
  height: 100vh;
}

/* Space distribution */
.nav {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between; /* items at edges, space in middle */
  gap: 16px;
}

/* flex-grow: let one item take remaining space */
.sidebar { width: 240px; flex-shrink: 0; }
.main    { flex-grow: 1; } /* fills remaining space */
Common Confusion

justify-content always controls alignment along the main axis, and align-items controls the cross axis. When you change flex-direction to column, the axes swap — so justify-content now controls vertical alignment. This trips people up frequently.

Follow-up

Use Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts — navigation bars, button groups, centering a single item. Use CSS Grid for two-dimensional layouts — page structure, card grids, dashboard panels. Flexbox and Grid are not mutually exclusive; it's common to use Grid for the page shell and Flexbox for individual components within it.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What is the difference between `align-items` and `align-self`?
    align-items is set on the flex container and applies to all children. align-self is set on an individual flex item and overrides the container's align-items for that item only. Use align-self when one item needs different cross-axis alignment than the rest.
  2. 2What does `flex: 1` shorthand actually set?

question: What is HTTP and what are the most common HTTP methods?
expectedPoints: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a stateless request–response protocol: the client sends a request with a method, URL, headers, and optional body; the server replies with a status code and optional body.
`GET` — read a resource; safe (no server-side effects) and idempotent; response may be cached by the browser; no request body allowed.
`POST` — submit data to create a resource; carries a request body; not idempotent (sending twice may create two records) and not safe.
`PUT` — replace a resource entirely (idempotent); `PATCH` — update a resource partially, only the supplied fields change; both require a request body.
`DELETE` — remove a resource; idempotent (calling it a second time leaves the server in the same state — resource is already absent).

Status code families: `2xx` success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), `3xx` redirect, `4xx` client error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found), `5xx` server error (500, 503).
followUps: What does idempotent mean in the context of HTTP?
What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
When would you use `PATCH` instead of `PUT`?
childExplanation: HTTP is the language browsers and servers use to talk to each other — like a standardised postal system for the web. Each HTTP method is like a type of request letter: GET says 'please send me this', POST says 'I'm sending you something new to store', PUT says 'replace this file with what I'm sending', PATCH says 'update just this part', and DELETE says 'throw this away'. The server always writes back with a status code — 200 means 'done', 404 means 'couldn't find it', 500 means 'I broke'.
detailedExplanation:
HTTP Methods

HTTP is a stateless request–response protocol. The client sends a request with a method, URL, headers, and optional body; the server replies with a status code and optional body. Each method has a defined semantic and two key properties: safety (does it modify server state?) and idempotency (does repeating the call produce the same result?).

// GET — read a resource; no request body
fetch('/api/users/1');

// POST — create a resource; body required; NOT idempotent
fetch('/api/users', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Alice' }),
});

// PATCH — partial update (only supplied fields change)
fetch('/api/users/1', {
  method: 'PATCH',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Bob' }), // other fields remain unchanged
});

// PUT — replace resource entirely
fetch('/api/users/1', {
  method: 'PUT',
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Bob', email: 'bob@example.com' }), // must include all fields
});

// DELETE — remove a resource; no body needed
fetch('/api/users/1', { method: 'DELETE' });

Idempotency & Safety

Key Concept

A safe method does not modify server state (GET, HEAD). An idempotent method produces the same server state no matter how many times it's called. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — calling DELETE twice leaves the server in the same state (resource is gone either way). POST is neither safe nor idempotent — sending it twice creates two resources. This matters for retry logic: it is safe to auto-retry GET or DELETE on a network failure, but retrying a POST may create duplicates.

Status Codes

Must-know codes

200 OK · 201 Created (successful POST) · 204 No Content (successful DELETE) · 400 Bad Request (invalid input) · 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated) · 403 Forbidden (authenticated but no permission) · 404 Not Found · 409 Conflict (e.g. duplicate) · 422 Unprocessable Entity (validation failed) · 500 Internal Server Error.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why are GET requests cached by the browser but POST requests are not?
    GET is defined as safe and idempotent — the same URL always returns the same resource, making it safe to cache. POST changes server state and the response depends on the request body, so caching it could return a stale or incorrect response. Browsers and CDN intermediaries follow the HTTP spec and do not cache POST by default.
  2. 2When would you use PATCH instead of PUT?
    Use PATCH when you only want to update specific fields of a resource without requiring the client to send the full representation. For example, changing just a user's email — with PUT the client must resend all fields (name, role, preferences…) or risk overwriting them with empty values. PATCH is also more bandwidth-efficient for large resources.
  3. 3What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
    401 means the request lacks valid authentication credentials — the server does not know who you are. The client should log in and retry. 403 means the server knows who you are but you do not have permission to access the resource — logging in again will not help. A common mistake is returning 401 for all auth failures regardless of whether the user is authenticated.
  4. 4What is the difference between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3?
    HTTP/1.1 processes one request per TCP connection at a time. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection using binary framing — eliminating application-layer head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC (UDP-based) for lower latency on lossy networks, since a dropped packet only blocks one stream instead of all.

question: What is the difference between CSS `position: relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, and `sticky`?
expectedPoints: `relative`: offset from its normal position; still occupies space in the document flow.
`absolute`: removed from document flow; positioned relative to the nearest positioned ancestor.
`fixed`: removed from flow; positioned relative to the viewport — stays in place on scroll.
`sticky`: hybrid — behaves like `relative` until a scroll threshold, then sticks like `fixed`.
A common pattern: wrap an absolutely positioned child inside a relatively positioned parent.
followUps: What is a stacking context and how does `z-index` relate to it?
When would you use `sticky` over `fixed`?
childExplanation: Think of elements as people sitting in rows. A `relative` person slides their chair a bit without leaving their spot — the chair space is still 'reserved'. An `absolute` person gets up and hovers above everyone else, anchored to the nearest person who 'claimed their space' (a positioned ancestor). A `fixed` person floats and is nailed to a specific corner of the window — they don't move when you scroll. A `sticky` person sits normally until the row scrolls past a certain point, then they grab the window edge and stick there.
detailedExplanation:
CSS positioning controls how an element is placed in the document. The default is position: static (normal flow). Any other value creates a positioned element that can be a containing block for absolute descendants.

/* relative — stays in flow, offset with top/left/etc. */
.badge {
  position: relative;
  top: -4px; /* shifts up 4px, space still reserved */
}

/* absolute — anchors to nearest positioned ancestor */
.parent { position: relative; } /* creates the anchor */
.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  top: 0; right: 0; /* top-right corner of .parent */
}

/* fixed — nailed to the viewport */
.navbar {
  position: fixed;
  top: 0; left: 0; right: 0;
}

/* sticky — relative until threshold, then sticks */
.section-header {
  position: sticky;
  top: 60px; /* sticks 60px from top of viewport */
}
Common Mistake

Forgetting to set position: relative on the parent when using position: absolute on a child. Without a positioned ancestor, the absolute element anchors to the nearest positioned ancestor — often the <html> element — causing it to jump to an unexpected position on the page.

Follow-up

z-index only works on positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky). Higher values stack on top. Elements create a new stacking context under certain conditions (opacity < 1, transform, filter, etc.), which can cause z-index to behave unexpectedly — a child's z-index is always relative to its stacking context, not the global document.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why does `sticky` sometimes stop working?
    Sticky positioning requires a scrolling ancestor — a parent with overflow: auto/scroll/hidden can clip the sticky element or prevent it from sticking to the viewport. If any ancestor has overflow: hidden, the sticky element cannot escape that clipping context. The element also stops sticking when it reaches the bottom of its parent, which is the intended behaviour (it doesn't stick past its containing block).
  2. 2What creates a new stacking context, and why does it break `z-index`?
    A new stacking context is created by: position with a z-index value other than auto, opacity less than 1, transform, filter, will-change, and others. Inside a stacking context, z-index values are relative to that context — a child with z-index: 9999 inside a low-priority context can still render below elements in a higher-priority parent context. This is why a modal inside a transformed container can appear behind other elements.

question: What is lazy loading and how does it improve web performance?
expectedPoints: Lazy loading defers loading of non-critical resources until they are needed.
For images: the `loading="lazy"` attribute defers off-screen images.
For JavaScript: dynamic `import()` loads a module only when required, reducing initial bundle size.
Benefits: faster initial page load, lower bandwidth usage, better Time to Interactive (TTI).
Trade-off: a short delay when the resource is eventually needed.
followUps: What is the difference between lazy loading and code splitting?
How does `React.lazy` work?
childExplanation: Imagine a restaurant that only cooks your dessert after you finish your main course, instead of having everything ready on the table from the start. This keeps the kitchen (browser) from doing unnecessary work upfront and makes the experience feel faster — your main course (above-the-fold content) arrives quickly. Lazy loading is the same idea: only load images and code when the user actually needs them.
detailedExplanation:
Lazy loading defers fetching resources until the moment they are needed, reducing the amount of data downloaded and work done during initial page load.

<!-- Lazy image — browser loads only when near viewport -->
<img
  src="/hero.jpg"
  loading="lazy"       <-- native browser attribute
  width="800"
  height="600"        <-- always set to prevent CLS
  alt="Hero image"
/>

// Dynamic import — load JS module on demand
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const { openModal } = await import('./modal.js');
  openModal();
});

// React.lazy — lazy load a component
const Chart = React.lazy(() => import('./Chart'));
// <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Chart /></Suspense>
CLS Warning

Always specify width and height on lazy-loaded images. Without them the browser does not know the image dimensions before it loads, so surrounding content shifts when the image appears — causing Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), a Core Web Vital that affects your Google ranking.

Follow-up

Code splitting is the mechanism (splitting the JavaScript bundle into multiple chunks). Lazy loading is the strategy (loading those chunks on demand). Dynamic import() achieves both simultaneously. Bundlers like Webpack and Vite automatically create separate chunk files for each dynamic import.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1What is the difference between `loading="lazy"` and IntersectionObserver?
    loading="lazy" is a native browser attribute that delegates image deferral entirely to the browser — zero JavaScript required. IntersectionObserver is a JavaScript API you use for custom lazy loading logic — for example, swapping a low-quality placeholder with the full image only when it enters the viewport, or triggering infinite scroll data fetching. The native attribute is preferred for standard images; IntersectionObserver for custom behaviour.
  2. 2Should you lazy load above-the-fold images?
    No. Above-the-fold images (visible without scrolling) should load as fast as possible — lazy loading them would delay the LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) metric. Add loading="eager" (or omit the attribute) and consider <link rel="preload"> for hero images. Only use loading="lazy" on images that are initially off-screen.

question: What is a render-blocking resource and how do you deal with it?
expectedPoints: A render-blocking resource must be fully downloaded and parsed before the browser can display content.
CSS in `<head>` is render-blocking by default.
JavaScript in `<head>` without `defer` or `async` is parser-blocking and render-blocking.
`defer`: downloads in parallel, executes after HTML is parsed, in order.
`async`: downloads in parallel, executes immediately when ready (may interrupt parsing).
Inline critical CSS in `<head>` to unblock above-the-fold rendering.
followUps: What is the difference between `async` and `defer`?
What is critical CSS?
childExplanation: Imagine your browser is a painter trying to paint a wall. A render-blocking resource is like a delivery that the painter refuses to start without — even if the delivery has nothing to do with painting the first section of the wall. CSS and JS files loaded in the `<head>` are like mandatory deliveries. Using `defer` is like telling the painter 'you can start while the delivery is on its way — just don't use it until it arrives.' Using `async` is even more relaxed: 'use it the second it arrives, even if you're mid-stroke'.
detailedExplanation:
The browser builds the DOM (from HTML) and CSSOM (from CSS) before it can render anything. Any resource that blocks either of these delays the First Contentful Paint (FCP).

<!-- ✗ Blocks parsing AND rendering -->
<script src="app.js"></script>

<!-- ✓ defer: parallel download, runs after HTML parsed, in order -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

<!-- ✓ async: parallel download, runs as soon as ready (no order guarantee) -->
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>

<!-- ✓ CSS: inline critical styles, load rest non-blocking -->
<style>/* above-the-fold styles only */</style>
<link rel="preload" href="styles.css" as="style"
  onload="this.rel='stylesheet'">
async vs defer

defer is usually the right choice for application scripts — it preserves execution order and runs after the DOM is ready. Use async only for independent scripts like analytics or ads where execution order does not matter and you want the absolute fastest execution. Never use async for scripts that depend on each other.

Follow-up

Critical CSS is the minimal set of CSS rules needed to render the above-the-fold content. Inlining it in a <style> tag in the <head> eliminates a render-blocking network request, improving FCP. The rest of the CSS can load non-blockingly. Tools like critical (npm) or Lighthouse can help identify what critical CSS to extract.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why does placing scripts at the bottom of `` help, and is it still needed with `defer`?
    Placing scripts at the bottom of <body> lets the browser parse the full HTML before encountering the script, preventing parser blocking. With defer, the script downloads in parallel and executes after the HTML is parsed regardless of where the tag appears — so the bottom-of-body trick is no longer needed. Use defer in <head> instead for cleaner markup.
  2. 2What is `rel="preload"` and how does it differ from `defer`?
    rel="preload" tells the browser to fetch a resource as early as possible but not to execute or apply it immediately — it just warms the cache. defer is specifically for scripts and controls both download timing and execution order. Use preload for fonts, images, or CSS you know you'll need soon; use defer for scripts that need the DOM ready.

quiz.question: Which `<script>` attribute downloads in parallel with HTML parsing and executes after the HTML is fully parsed, preserving script order?
quiz.explanation: `defer` downloads the script in parallel without blocking HTML parsing, and executes all deferred scripts in order after the HTML parse is complete. `async` also downloads in parallel but executes immediately when ready — interrupting parsing and with no order guarantee. `lazy` and `preload` are not valid `<script>` attributes.

question: What is the difference between unit tests and integration tests?
expectedPoints: Unit tests verify a single function or component in isolation, with external dependencies mocked.
Integration tests verify that multiple units work correctly together.
Unit tests are fast and pinpoint failures precisely; integration tests catch wiring bugs.
End-to-end (E2E) tests exercise the full application through a real browser.
The testing pyramid recommends many unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewer still E2E tests.
followUps: What is the testing pyramid?
When would you prefer an integration test over a unit test?
childExplanation: Unit tests are like testing each individual car part in isolation — check that the engine starts, that each door handle works, that each window rolls down. Integration tests check that the parts work together — does the key turn, which triggers the engine, which moves the wheels? You need both: isolated part tests catch problems within each component, while integration tests catch problems in how they connect.
detailedExplanation:
Different test types offer different trade-offs between speed, isolation, and confidence. Knowing when to use each is a key engineering skill.

// Unit test — tests one function in isolation
// (Jest example)
test('formatCurrency formats dollars correctly', () => {
  expect(formatCurrency(1234.5)).toBe('$1,234.50');
});

// Integration test — tests a form + validation + API together
// (React Testing Library)
test('submitting the login form calls the auth API', async () => {
  render(<LoginForm />);
  userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText('Email'), 'alice@example.com');
  userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' }));
  await waitFor(() =>
    expect(mockAuthApi).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ email: 'alice@example.com' })
  );
});
Test Ice Cream vs Pyramid

The 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern is the opposite of the pyramid: many manual and E2E tests at the top, few unit tests at the bottom. E2E tests are slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain. Invest heavily in unit tests (fast, precise), moderately in integration tests (real confidence), and sparingly in E2E (smoke tests for critical paths only).

Follow-up

React Testing Library deliberately makes it harder to write unit tests that test implementation details (directly accessing component state or internal methods). It encourages integration-style tests that interact with the component through the UI — clicking buttons and checking visible text — giving higher confidence that the component works as a user would use it.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why should you test behaviour, not implementation details?
    Tests that assert internal state (variable values, private method calls) break every time you refactor, even when the observable behaviour is unchanged. Tests tied to behaviour (what the user sees and interacts with) survive refactoring — they only fail when something the user would notice actually breaks. This gives you a safety net that enables confident refactoring rather than one that punishes it.
  2. 2What makes a test "flaky" and how do you fix it?
    A flaky test passes sometimes and fails sometimes without code changes — usually caused by: real timers (use fake timers), network calls (mock the API), shared mutable state between tests (reset it in beforeEach/afterEach), or relying on DOM rendering timing (use waitFor / findBy). Flaky tests destroy trust in the test suite — fix or delete them.

question: What is mocking in tests and why is it useful?
expectedPoints: Mocking replaces a real dependency with a fake that returns controlled values.
Makes tests fast and deterministic — no real network or filesystem calls.
Allows testing error cases that are hard to trigger with real services.
In Jest: `jest.fn()` mocks functions; `jest.mock('module')` mocks entire modules.
Over-mocking leads to brittle tests — mock at the boundary, not everywhere.
followUps: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, and a spy?
How do you test a component that fetches data from an API?
childExplanation: Flight simulators let pilots train for emergencies without risking real planes or passengers. The simulator is a 'mock' of a real aircraft — it behaves the same way but runs in a controlled environment. In testing, mocking swaps out real dependencies (APIs, databases, clocks) for controllable fakes. This lets you simulate 'the server returned a 500 error' or 'it is midnight on New Year's Eve' without actually breaking the server or waiting for midnight.
detailedExplanation:
Mocks let you isolate the code under test by replacing its collaborators with controllable substitutes. This makes tests fast, deterministic, and able to cover error paths.

// jest.fn() — mock a function, track calls
const onSubmit = jest.fn();
render(<Form onSubmit={onSubmit} />);
userEvent.click(screen.getByText('Submit'));
expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

// jest.mock() — mock an entire module
jest.mock('../api', () => ({
  fetchUser: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }),
}));

// Simulating an error
fetchUser.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('Network error'));
// Now test that your component shows an error state

// jest.spyOn() — wrap a real function to track calls
const spy = jest.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {});
// ... do something that might log errors
expect(spy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
Over-mocking

Mocking too much creates tests that pass even when the real system is broken — the tests only verify that your mocks work, not your code. Mock at the boundary: real network calls, database connections, timers, random numbers. Let real application logic run without mocking. The closer your test environment is to production, the more confidence the tests give.

Follow-up

Mock: replaces a dependency entirely with a fake. Stub: a simplified implementation that returns a fixed value (often used interchangeably with mock). Spy: wraps the real implementation and records calls — you can assert how many times a function was called and with what arguments, while still running the real logic.

🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How do you use MSW (Mock Service Worker) instead of `jest.mock` for API calls?
    MSW intercepts real HTTP requests at the network level using a Service Worker (in browser) or Node.js interceptors (in tests). You define request handlers (http.get('/api/users', resolver)) and MSW returns the mocked response. Unlike jest.mock, your application code uses the real fetch/axios — only the network is intercepted. This means tests exercise more real code paths while still controlling responses.
  2. 2When should you test error states, and how do you trigger them?
    Always test error states for any operation that can fail — API calls, form validation, permission checks. Mock the dependency to throw or reject: mockFetchUser.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('500')). Then assert that the component shows an appropriate error message rather than crashing. Error paths are often undertested and are where real bugs live in production.

options: It makes the test more realistic by using the real server

question: Tell me about a project you're proud of. What was your contribution and what did you learn?
expectedPoints: Describes a specific project with clear context (what it was, who it was for).
Clearly articulates their individual contribution vs the team's work.
Mentions a concrete challenge they overcame during the project.
Reflects on what they learned — technically or about working with others.
Delivers the answer in a structured way (Situation, Task, Action, Result).
followUps: What would you do differently if you started that project today?
How did you handle disagreements with teammates on that project?
childExplanation: Interviewers ask this question to understand three things at once: what you've actually built, how you think about your own work, and whether you can communicate clearly. The best answers are specific (a real project, not a vague description), personal (your role, not just 'we did everything'), and reflective (what you learned, not just what you shipped). Use the STAR structure to stay organised: Situation → Task → Action → Result.
detailedExplanation:
This is one of the most common early-career interview questions. The interviewer wants to see evidence of real work, self-awareness, and communication — not a perfect project.

STAR Structure

  • Situation: What was the context? (Team size, timeline, type of project — personal, school, internship, open source)
  • Task: What was your specific responsibility?
  • Action: What did you do? Be specific — name the technologies, describe the decisions you made.
  • Result: What was the outcome? If measurable (performance improvement, user count, grade) even better. If not, describe what shipped and what you learned.

Strong Answer Traits

  • Specific: "I built a REST API with Node.js and Express that handled image uploads" beats "I worked on the backend."
  • Honest about scope: Junior roles rarely own entire systems — owning one feature or component is perfectly fine.
  • Includes a challenge: "The hardest part was X. I solved it by Y." This signals problem-solving ability.
  • Self-aware learning: "Looking back, I'd now do Z differently" shows maturity.
Common Mistakes

Describing a group project as if you did everything alone (interviewers probe this and it backfires). Describing a project so vaguely the interviewer can't picture it. Failing to explain the technical choices you made. Ending without a result or learning.

Follow-up Prep

Be ready for: "Why did you choose that technology?" / "What would you improve?" / "How did you test it?" / "What was the biggest challenge?" If you can answer these naturally, you clearly owned the project — not just read about it.

🪜 Self-Interview Practice

Answer before reading guidance.

  1. 1What if you haven't worked on a professional project yet?
    Personal, academic, and open-source projects are all valid. A todo app you built to learn React, a university assignment where you implemented a graph algorithm, or a small contribution to an open-source repo — any of these work. The key is that you can speak in depth about what you built, why you made certain decisions, and what you'd improve. Lack of professional experience is expected at the junior level.
  2. 2How long should this answer be?
    Aim for 2–3 minutes. Cover the STAR structure but don't read every detail — leave room for the interviewer to ask follow-up questions. Speak clearly and at a moderate pace. If you finish quickly (under 90 seconds), you probably weren't specific enough. If you go over 4 minutes, you're over-explaining — practise trimming.
